---
title: "Creating a Diagram"
format: html
---
Data can be visualized using many plotting libraries (e.g. `Plots`, `Makie`, etc.). We will be introducing `Plots` here, as it offers a certain simplicity when creating a plot.

First we need to add the package (look at Chapter Packages on how to do so). Then we can load the package in our code:
```{julia}
using Plots
```
Now we can start to visualize some data!

## Line plot
Let's start by defining some variables we will use for plotting.
```{julia}
#| output: false
x = LinRange(0,10,100)
y = 2 * x.^2
```
Here we have a 100-element vector for `x` and an expression for `y`. Note the element-wise operation on `x`. This generates a 100-element vector for `y` with each element being an expression of the corresponding element of `x`. To plot this data as a line, you can use the `plot()` function included in `Plots`.
```{julia}
#| label: fig-parabola1
plot(y)
```
```{julia}
#| label: fig-parabola2
plot(x,y)
```
As you can see, `plot()` can take several arguments `plot(y)` will use the input as the y-axis and use a unit-rage for the x-axis. `plot(x,y)` will use the first argument as the x-axis and the second as the y-axis.

We can also start tweaking the appearance of the plot by adding labels to the axes and removing the label as we are only plotting one dataset:
```{julia}
#| label: fig-sine
x = LinRange(0,2pi,181)
y = sin.(x)

plot(x,y, xlabel="x", ylabel="y", label=false)
```

## Scatter plot
But what if the data doesn't fit along a line but scatters? We can also use a scatter plot to visualize the data points individually. `scatter()` works analogously to `plot()`:

```{julia}
#| label: fig-scatter
x =  randn(181)
y =  randn(181)

scatter(x,y, xlabel="x", ylabel="y", label=false)
```

## Heat map
Oftentimes however, we do not have data that can be visualized on a two-dimensional line or scatter plot (2D spatial distribution of a quantity). In that case we need two dimensions to parametrize the space, and a third dimension to parametrize the quantity.
Let's define two independent vectors for the x- and y-axis, as well as an expression for a heat perturbation depending on both x and y:
```{julia}
#| output: flase
x =  LinRange(-50,50,200)
y =  LinRange(-50,50,200)
T =  exp.(-((1.5*x').^2 .+ y.^2) / (2*(15^2))) # gaussian function
```
As we want T to be a two-dimensional array, we need to make sure to transpose `x` in the expression, as both `x` and `y` are defined as column vectors.
To visualize this data we can still use a two-dimensional plot and plot the heat distribution as colours. This is called a `heatmap()` and can again take many arguments, `heatmap(x,y,z)` will use x as input for the x-axis, y for the y-axis and z for the colouring:
```{julia}
#| label: fig-heatmap
heatmap(x,y,T, xlabel="x", ylabel="y", aspect_ratio=1, xlims=extrema(x), ylims=extrema(y))
```
You should always make sure to check the resulting heatmap if it makes sense, as it is easy to forget transposing correctly.
## Contour plot
The contour plot is similar to the heatmap but will only plot lines at certain values of `z`:
```{julia}
#| label: fig-contour
contour(x,y,T, xlabel="x", ylabel="y", aspect_ratio=1, xlims=extrema(x), ylims=extrema(y))
```

## Other projections
Aside from a Cartesian coordinate system, we can also plot some data using a polar projection by setting the argument `proj` to polar
```{julia}
#| label: fig-polar
θ = LinRange(0,2pi,181)
r = abs.(sin.(4θ))

plot(θ, r, proj=:polar, xlabel="x", ylabel="y", label=false)
```
